issues.description: The problem statement and UML specify that SealSaloon has a shared, final field of type Stock (the inventory type) and describe Stock methods (add/take/findStockIngredient/addToStockIngredients/emptyStock). However, the provided template and solution repositories supply a fully implemented class named Inventory with those methods, and the Stock.java file in the template/solution is empty. In the solution SealSaloon implementation the stock field is declared as type Inventory (line 5 of SealSaloon.java) rather than Stock. This type/name mismatch between the expected type 'Stock' (problem/UML) and the actual type 'Inventory' (template/solution) will cause compilation errors or confusion if students follow the problem text literally.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the inventory type consistent across problem text, templates, and solution. Two viable fixes: (A) Rename the provided Inventory class and its usages to Stock (update class name and file to Stock.java, remove the empty Stock.java placeholder), ensuring it implements the methods referenced in the UML; or (B) Update the problem statement and UML to refer to 'Inventory' (change all mentions of final Stock and the UML node) so that the expected type matches the provided class. Apply the chosen change in all artifacts (problem text, UML, template files, and example solution) so SealSaloon.stock has the same declared type everywhere.

issues.description: The problem statement and UML use the identifier 'Stock' for the saloon's inventory type (including UML edges that label the SealSaloon.stock attribute as Stock), but the template and solution code use the identifier 'Inventory' for the same concept and provide an Inventory.java with the expected methods. Having the same concept named 'Stock' in the specification and 'Inventory' in the codebase creates a naming inconsistency that will confuse students about which class to implement or use and may lead them to create duplicate implementations.
issues.suggestedFix: Unify the identifier for the inventory concept across all materials. Either (1) rename Inventory.java and all references to 'Inventory' to 'Stock' (and remove the empty Stock.java), or (2) revise the problem statement and UML to use 'Inventory' instead of 'Stock' (including changing the UML attribute types and the text that says 'final Stock'). Ensure the chosen name is used consistently in the template, solution, and problem description to avoid student confusion.
